items.videoDescription:
Ever found an amazing animation on a website and wished you could recreate it in your own project?

Not just something similar. The actual movement, timing, transitions, and visual effects.

Meet /reanimate, a new open-source Claude Code skill that reverse-engineers animations frame by frame and rebuilds them directly in your code.

And the results are pretty impressive.

Here's how it works:

Capture: Give Claude a website URL, screen recording, MP4, or GIF containing the animation you want.

Analyze: The skill extracts movement, timing, easing curves, element positions, and visual properties frame by frame.

Rebuild: Claude recreates the animation using your existing technology stack, including CSS, Framer Motion, GSAP, or Three.js.

Compare: It records the recreated animation and compares it against the original.

Refine: The agent identifies differences and automatically iterates until the result meets its target or reports remaining issues.

And here's where things get really interesting.

This isn't limited to simple CSS transitions.

Reanimate can inspect complex graphics built with:

Three.js: Interactive 3D scenes and animations

WebGL and WebGPU: GPU-powered visual effects

Canvas: Procedural graphics and particle systems

GSAP and Framer Motion: Complex timelines, transitions, and interactive effects

The skill can even trace shaders, GPU rendering calls, and animated properties to understand how sophisticated visual effects work.

But how accurate is it?

According to the project's own demonstrations:

A complex 3D cube animation recreated with 0.11% pixel difference

Interactive feature cards with less than 0.6% difference

A particle-based star animation with just 0.014% difference during a click effect

These are developer-reported examples, not guaranteed results for every animation.

The skill's pixel-perfect mode targets a mean pixel mismatch of 2% or less.

And unlike simply generating a video that looks similar, the result is actual editable code you can integrate into your project.

Install /reanimate:

npx skills add NiazMorshed2007/reanimate -g

Then open Claude Code and try something like:

/reanimate the hero animation from https://example.com into components/Hero.tsx

You'll need Bun 1.1+ on macOS or Linux. The first run also downloads Chromium and FFmpeg.

The project is free and open source under the MIT license. Remember to respect the original creators' rights when reusing visual assets.

And here's why I find this particularly exciting.

Until recently, recreating a sophisticated website animation meant spending hours studying the original, guessing how it worked, and manually tweaking countless tiny details.

Now an AI coding agent can record, analyze, reconstruct, and visually verify the entire process.

We're moving from AI that copies what a website looks like to AI that can reconstruct how it moves.

That's a pretty significant step for creative coding and frontend development.

And a potentially dangerous development for anyone hoping their beautiful website animation will remain unique for long.

Live demonstrations:

items.videoDescription:
What if you could turn dozens of scientific research papers into an interactive laboratory you can actually experiment with?

Not just summaries. Not another chatbot explaining complicated equations.

Actual working simulations built directly from published research.

A fascinating Claude Code experiment attributed to Boris Cherny, the creator of Claude Code, shows what happens when you give 12 AI agents 64 scientific papers about fluid dynamics and ask them to build a browser-based laboratory.

And the result is beautiful.

Here's what the agents reportedly created:

Interactive fluid simulations: Choose different experiments and watch physical phenomena unfold.

Adjustable parameters: Change conditions using sliders and immediately see how the results respond.

Multiple simulation methods: Compare different approaches using the same experimental settings.

Scientific references: Explore equations, source code, and measurements alongside each animation.

Research verification: Compare simulation outputs with the results reported in the original papers.

But here's the really interesting part.

The agents didn't all work on the same problem.

They had specialized responsibilities.

Research agents extracted equations, assumptions, and experimental parameters from the papers.

Development agents translated those methods into working simulation code.

Interface agents built the interactive controls and visualizations.

Review agents checked the implementations against the original research, looking for numerical errors, instability, and discrepancies.

According to the circulated demonstration, the project covered 11 simulation methods across 28 reference scenarios, with seven meeting the selected validation tolerances and four requiring further review.

Those figures are reported rather than independently verified.

And that distinction matters.

A beautiful simulation isn't necessarily a scientifically accurate simulation.

But imagine applying this workflow to your own research.

A collection of scientific papers becomes an interactive environment where you can test assumptions, compare methods, adjust variables, and inspect the underlying code.

Want to try something similar?

Here's a prompt you can adapt for Claude Code:

"Turn these research papers into an interactive browser-based laboratory.

Extract the methods, equations, assumptions, and experimental parameters from each paper, including page references.

Assign different methods to specialized agents, using shared inputs and measurement tools so the results can be compared.

Have independent review agents verify each implementation against the original paper. Document discrepancies and clearly mark unverified results.

Build an interactive interface with parameter sliders, visual simulations, method comparisons, and access to the source code behind each experiment.

Make the experiments reproducible, including their dependencies, reference data, and validation procedures."

Start with one paper and one experiment, verify the results, and expand from there.

And here's what I find genuinely exciting.

We're moving beyond AI that simply reads research papers and tells us what they say.

We're approaching a world where AI agents can help turn scientific knowledge into working, explorable software.

From reading science to experimenting with it.

That's a much more interesting use of AI than generating another thousand summaries nobody will ever read.

Autonomous tracking: Identify and follow a moving person without continuous manual steering.

No GPS required: Navigate without relying on satellite positioning.

We're entering an era where AI-powered machines can perceive their surroundings, make navigation decisions, and physically pursue moving targets.

Without waiting for instructions from a remote server.

Of course, this is still an experimental research demonstration, not proof that autonomous drones can reliably track anyone under all conditions.

But watching that little machine weave between trees while following a human is enough to make you wonder where all this is heading.

What if you could type using a font inspired by Michelangelo's own handwriting?

Well, now you can.

Meet Michelangelus, a beautiful new serif typeface created by Italian design studio Studiogusto, inspired by the handwriting of Renaissance master Michelangelo Buonarroti.

And the story behind it is just as fascinating as the design itself.

The designers studied more than 300 original manuscripts, examining Michelangelo's letters, signatures, proportions, and distinctive writing style.

But they didn't simply copy his handwriting.

They transformed it into an entirely new, carefully constructed digital typeface.

Here's where the inspiration came from:

Lowercase letters: Based on Michelangelo's handwritten manuscripts and personal correspondence.

Capital letters: Inspired by his signature on the Pietà and the monumental inscription on St. Peter's Basilica.

Four styles: Regular, Italic, Bold, and Bold Italic.

500+ glyphs: Latin characters, ligatures, stylistic alternates, numbers, fractions, and symbols.

Special characters: Currency symbols, religious marks, historical symbols, and decorative letterforms.

And here's another interesting detail.

Michelangelus was commissioned by the Vatican's Fabbrica di San Pietro and developed in collaboration with Microsoft.

The typeface was designed to bring Renaissance craftsmanship into modern digital communication, including Microsoft 365.

items.videoDescription:
Anthropic just entered the race for the ultimate personal AI assistant.

Meet Claude Duet, a new proactive AI agent powered by Claude Opus 5.5.

And unlike regular Claude, this one doesn't just sit around waiting for your prompts.

It actually comes to you first.

Claude Duet monitors your connected apps, identifies things that need attention, sends morning briefings, and works on tasks in the background, even when your computer is turned off.

Here's what makes it interesting:

Claude Opus 5.5: Anthropic's powerful reasoning model handles the work.

One ongoing conversation: Your tasks, questions, and projects live in a single continuous chat.

Proactive monitoring: Duet checks connected apps every few hours and alerts you when something matters.

Background execution: Its own virtual computer and browser let it work independently of your devices.

6,000+ connectors and plugins: Access tools through Claude Marketplace, including Gmail, Slack, Notion, Stripe, Shopify, and more.

AI-powered shopping: Duet can purchase products using Stripe Link or Shopify Shop Pay, with your approval.

You can ask it to manage emails, prepare financial reports, build dashboards, schedule meetings, develop web apps, or simply figure out what deserves your attention today.

But there's something I find a little strange.

Anthropic chose a single-agent experience built around one never-ending conversation.

Personally, I'm not entirely convinced this is better than having multiple specialized agents working on different projects.

We've already seen similar debates around OpenAI's Dots.

And then there's the security.

In true Anthropic fashion, Claude Duet comes with an impressive collection of safeguards:

The agent never directly sees your passwords or authentication tokens.

A dedicated safety classifier protects sensitive information.

Sending messages, making payments, signing documents, and deleting data require your approval.

Trading stocks and transferring money between accounts are prohibited, even with permission.

So yes, your AI assistant can help run your business.

It just can't become your personal hedge fund manager.

There's another catch.

Claude Duet shares usage limits with your regular Claude subscription, including the tokens consumed by background tasks.

And while the 6,000+ integrations sound impressive, that's the broader Marketplace catalog, not a guarantee that every integration works perfectly in Duet today.

Availability:

Claude Duet is launching as a research preview on iOS, Android, and the web.

For now, access is limited to US subscribers on Claude Pro and Max plans, through a waitlist.

Still, I'm genuinely curious about this one.

Opus 5.5 is a powerful foundation for an autonomous agent, and Anthropic's approach to combining reasoning, persistent context, and background execution could make Duet a serious competitor to OpenAI Dots, Meta Muse, and other proactive assistants.

The AI assistant wars are getting interesting.

And apparently, the next big feature isn't answering your questions.

It's knowing what you need before you even ask.

What if an AI coding agent helped discover a planet that astronomers had missed for seven years?
And what if NASA actually agreed to investigate?
That's exactly what's happening.
Independent researcher Pavel Rabtsevich used Claude Code and OpenAI Codex to analyze archived data from NASA's TESS space telescope.
The result? A possible new exoplanet orbiting a star approximately 116 light-years from Earth.

Here's what the AI-assisted investigation uncovered:
- A star called TIC 4206066
- A mysterious 0.05% drop in brightness every 3.18 days
- Each dip lasts approximately two hours
- The signal is consistent with a planet roughly 1.4 times Earth's radius
- Similar signals appear in telescope data collected years apart

Claude Code handled much of the technical work: processing telescope data, writing transit-detection algorithms, analyzing light curves, checking neighboring stars, and testing alternative explanations.

The human researcher directed the investigation, challenged the results, and established the criteria for success or failure.
And here's where it gets really interesting.

NASA's TESS mission has approved follow-up observations under Director's Discretionary Target Program 100. The observations are scheduled for October 31 to November 26, 2026. tess.mit.edu

The planet isn't confirmed yet. The signal could have another explanation, and that's precisely what the new observations will investigate.
But the implications are fascinating.

We're watching AI coding agents move beyond generating software and into actual scientific research.

One researcher. Public NASA data. A few AI agents. And possibly an entirely new world.

items.videoDescription:
Apparently, someone decided that smartphones weren't enough.

We now need screens in our sweaters.

Researchers at the National University of Singapore have developed a fully functional color touchscreen woven directly into clothing.

And no, they didn't just glue a tiny display onto a sleeve.

The electronics are literally inside the threads.

Here's what they've managed to create:

54 electronic fibers, containing thousands of microscopic LEDs

96 × 54 pixel resolution, because apparently we're bringing 1990s graphics back

30 FPS video playback, directly on your sleeve

Full-color touchscreen, supporting multiple simultaneous touches

Working apps, including a calculator, compass, and photo gallery

Bluetooth connectivity, voice commands, and temperature monitoring

50 machine washes, with little loss of display or touch functionality

And somehow, the fabric remains flexible and breathable.

The really impressive part is the engineering.

Each fiber contains tiny electronic components that work together to create a display and detect touch.

So instead of wearing a device, the clothing itself becomes the interface.

Of course, it's still a laboratory prototype.

The resolution is terrible, the electronics need external power and controllers, and nobody has explained why watching a video on your forearm is better than simply taking your phone out of your pocket.

But who cares?

You can now watch gloriously pixelated memes on your sweater.

Humanity has spent decades making screens smaller. Now we're weaving them into knitwear.

And here's the inevitable next step.

We've already got phones, watches, headphones, and glasses that need charging.

Soon your sweater will ask you to plug it in before going to bed.

Welcome to the future of wearable technology.

What if you could take a viral video, give it to an AI, and turn it into an actual video game?
Not just a visual recreation. A fully explorable 3D world.
And what if the entire process took just 40 minutes?

About a year ago, a video featuring an enormous, seemingly endless fortress went viral on Twitter.
Yesterday, I gave that video to Claude Opus 5.5, connected it to an AI image generator for creating assets, provided specialized Three.js development skills, and asked for one thing:
"Build me a game like this. But make it possible to actually reach the roof of the fortress."
And Claude took the assignment rather seriously.
First, it analyzed the original video and calculated what exploring this massive structure would actually involve.

The results were ridiculous:
- 2.2 kilometers of walking to reach the roof
- 46 minutes at normal walking speed
- Two movement modes: walking and sprinting with Shift
- A fully explorable fortress with interconnected interior spaces
Then it built the game.

What Claude created in approximately 40 minutes:
- A playable 3D fortress inspired by the original video
- Procedurally assembled architecture and explorable interiors
- AI-generated visual assets
- A physics and movement system
- Original background music
- Walking and sprinting mechanics
- A guided navigation system that automatically leads you to the roof

All running directly in your browser.
No traditional game development pipeline. No manually building hundreds of rooms. Just Claude Opus 5.5, Three.js, AI-generated assets, and a prompt.
And here's what I find most interesting.

We're getting dangerously close to the era of personal video games.
See something interesting on the internet? Turn it into a game.
Want to explore a fictional world? Generate it.
Wish your favorite game had different mechanics, environments, or an entirely new storyline? Just ask.
Of course, this experiment still has bugs. I could spend another few hours adding gameplay mechanics, improving the environments, and polishing everything.
But I think I'll stop here.
Because the interesting part isn't whether the game is perfect.
It's that a single person can now turn a random internet video into an explorable world in less than an hour.

What if AI could generate an entire world while you're exploring it?

Not a video. Not a traditional game. An interactive reality that reacts to everything you do.

And now it has sound. And people who actually talk back.

Meet Google DeepMind's Genie 4, the next generation of AI world models.

And this is getting dangerously close to science fiction.

In this video, I've brought together Google's official presentation and more than 10 demonstrations of AI-generated worlds.

From photorealistic environments to surreal landscapes, talking characters, and interactive simulations.

And the results are genuinely fascinating.

Here's what's new in Genie 4:

Real-time world generation: Explore environments that continuously evolve as you move.

Native AI audio: Hear footsteps, wind, water, environmental sounds, and music generated alongside the visuals.

Interactive dialogue: AI-generated characters can speak and respond to what's happening around them.

Live scene editing: Change the weather, introduce characters, or transform the environment using text prompts.

More realistic physics: Improved simulations of movement, collisions, and physical interactions.

More believable humans: Characters can move, react, and interact with their surroundings more naturally.

But here's where things get really interesting.

Genie 4 doesn't work alone.

Google connected it to Gemini 3.8 Flash, which acts as a reasoning agent inside the simulation.

Gemini observes the generated world, breaks complex tasks into smaller steps, checks the results, and adjusts its plans when something changes.

In one demonstration, Google even shows a simulated Apollo humanoid robot playing checkers, using Gemini 4 Argon and Genie 4 together.

And this reveals something important.

Google isn't building these worlds just so we can play games.

World models are part of its long-term research toward artificial general intelligence.

Robots and autonomous AI agents need environments where they can learn, experiment, make mistakes, and understand consequences.

And simulated worlds could be considerably cheaper and safer than testing every new behavior with physical robots.

Imagine training thousands of robots without smashing thousands of actual robots into actual walls.

But the creative possibilities are just as exciting.

Game developers could prototype entire interactive worlds.

Filmmakers could experiment with scenes before filming.

Designers could build explorable environments from simple prompts.

AI agents could practice complex tasks in simulated spaces.

And the rest of us could finally explore those bizarre places we remember from our dreams.

Of course, we're not living in The Matrix just yet.

Genie 4 still struggles with long-term consistency, complex physics, spatial accuracy, and details that gradually change during extended interactions.

items.videoDescription:
What if you could take apart a V8 engine, explore an aircraft's landing gear, or see exactly how a walking robot works?

Without touching a real machine.

Meet Teardown, a free, open-source Claude Code skill that transforms mechanical systems into interactive 3D simulations.

And the results look seriously impressive.

Instead of creating another static 3D model, Claude builds an entire interactive laboratory where you can disassemble machines, control individual mechanisms, and watch the physics unfold.

Here's what Teardown can do:

Interactive 3D models: Rotate, zoom, and explore machines from different angles.

Exploded views: Take mechanisms apart and examine individual components.

Working animations: Watch gears, pistons, actuators, and mechanical linkages move.

Live measurements: Monitor joint torque, mechanical loads, movement, and other parameters.

Independent controls: Isolate subsystems and experiment with their behavior.

Automated demonstrations: Generate guided tours and animated videos of the mechanisms.

And the fascinating part?

The 3D geometry is generated programmatically using Three.js.

No prebuilt CAD model required.

The project includes three complete examples:

V8 engine: Explore pistons, cylinders, and the four-stroke combustion cycle.

Cessna 337 landing gear: Watch the hydraulic mechanism retract the wheels.

Strandbeest: Explore the remarkable walking mechanism inspired by Theo Jansen's kinetic sculptures.

But here's what makes Teardown technically interesting.

Instead of animating dozens of components independently, Claude builds a mathematical model that controls the entire mechanism.

Take the aircraft landing gear.

One actuator moves a rack by 201 mm.

That rack drives a 32-tooth gear with a module of 4 mm, producing a pitch diameter of 128 mm.

Half the gear's pitch circumference is approximately 201 mm.

So the rack's movement corresponds to a 180-degree rotation.

And the gear, landing gear legs, animations, charts, and instrument readings all follow the same underlying calculation.

One mathematical model. An entire machine moving in sync.

That's the difference between making a convincing animation and attempting to simulate how a mechanism actually works.

Of course, there's a catch.

The quality depends heavily on your reference material.

The creator experimented with generating a pangolin, an armadillo, and a scorpion without providing proper anatomical references.

The results? Three rather primitive models.

But give Claude technical drawings, dimensions, and real mechanical specifications, and things get considerably more interesting.

Want to try it?

Install the skill:

npx skills add elvarofficial/teardown -g -a claude-code

Then install the required dependencies:

cd ~/.claude/skills/teardown
npm install
npx playwright install chromium

Open Claude Code and run:

/teardown

You'll need Node.js 20 or newer. Video rendering also requires FFmpeg, with Python 3 used for sound generation.

The skill is free and MIT licensed. Claude Code usage may still consume your subscription allowance.

And here's why I find this project exciting.

We're moving from AI that explains how machines work to AI that can build interactive environments where you can actually explore those explanations.

For engineering education, robotics, product design, and technical visualization, that's a fascinating direction.

Imagine turning an engineering textbook into an interactive mechanical laboratory.

Instead of just reading about how something works, you could take it apart and see for yourself.

What if your entire AI-powered content business operated from a tiny virtual city?

With a newsroom, a video studio, a post office, a café, and even a bank?

Meet Grok City, a fascinating experiment in multi-agent automation built around Grok Bots.

And yes, every AI agent has its own little office.

We've all seen automated content factories before.

AI finds trending topics, writes scripts, generates videos, adds captions, and publishes everything to social media.

But this one takes the concept a little further.

Six AI agents. Six different jobs. One connected workflow.

Here's who lives in the city:

Scout (Newsroom): Searches for emerging AI stories before they go viral.

Hook (Writers' Room): Creates three opening hooks, tests them with Grok, and lets the human choose the winner.

Reply (Café): Handles comments, community interactions, and sponsorship messages.

Reel (Studio): Creates and renders videos, then delivers them to the Post Office.

Post (Post Office): Publishes threads and videos to X. A tiny paper airplane even flies out when something gets posted.

Ledger (Bank): Tracks revenue and helps identify which content actually makes money.

And here's the interesting part.

Everything is connected through a single content pipeline.

From discovering a story to tracking the revenue it generates.

There's a live activity log showing what every agent is doing, where tasks are moving, and what has already been completed.

And when something requires human judgment?

It appears in a separate "Needs You" inbox.

Approve. Reject. Make a decision. Let the agents continue.

Now, do AI agents actually work faster because they live in an adorable virtual city?

Absolutely not.

The little buildings, walking characters, and animated handoffs are mostly visual decoration.

But they do something surprisingly useful.

They make a complicated multi-agent system understandable at a glance.

You can actually see how the content factory is organized, which agent owns each task, and how work moves through the pipeline.

That's valuable when your automation grows beyond a couple of scripts.

And I have to admit something.

I spent several months building something remarkably similar.

Not the city, obviously.

A multi-agent system for research, content opportunities, automation, performance tracking, and continuous improvement.

Unfortunately, I got a little too ambitious with the underlying architecture and the self-improvement mechanisms.

And never quite finished the whole thing.

Watching Grok City makes me think I should probably get back to it.

Although I'm definitely not adding a virtual city.

The agents have enough work already. They don't need office real estate.

items.videoDescription:
Remember when "cloud computing" was just a metaphor?

Well, Google is taking it rather literally.

On October 30, 2026, Google announced that its AI model Gemma 4 had successfully generated a response from orbit and transmitted it back to Earth.

And the first response?

A haiku.

Yes. We've reached the point where artificial intelligence is writing poetry in space.

Meet Project Suncatcher, Google's ambitious experiment to explore whether future AI data centers could operate in orbit, powered by solar energy.

Here's what happened:

October 1, 2026: Google launched its prototype satellite aboard a SpaceX rocket.

Onboard AI hardware: The satellite carries Google's data-center-class Tensor Processing Unit (TPU).

Onboard model: Google's open-weight Gemma 4.

First successful response: Engineers sent a prompt from Earth asking the model to write a haiku about being in space.

The result: Gemma processed the request in orbit and transmitted its poem back as the satellite passed over Svalbard, Norway.

The poem:

Blue marble below
Data streams in silent grace
Starlight feeds my core.

Google CEO Sundar Pichai called it a "Hello World" moment for Project Suncatcher.

But Google isn't alone in this race.

In November 2025, Starcloud launched an NVIDIA H100 GPU into orbit, later demonstrating AI training and inference in space.

Now Google has achieved its own milestone using a TPU rather than an NVIDIA GPU.

And here's where things get really interesting.

Google is exploring a future in which networks of solar-powered satellites could provide large-scale AI computing infrastructure.

Imagine orbital data centers connected by laser links, operating above Earth's atmosphere.

Of course, there are enormous engineering challenges:

Cooling powerful processors in a vacuum

Protecting chips from radiation

Maintaining high-bandwidth satellite connections

Launching, maintaining, and eventually replacing orbital hardware

Making the entire system economically viable

So no, Google hasn't built a fully operational space data center yet.

But it has demonstrated that an advanced AI model can respond to a prompt using data-center-class hardware in orbit.

Next milestone: two interconnected experimental satellites in 2027.

And if Starship eventually makes launching large quantities of computing hardware economically practical, things could get very interesting.

I suppose one day I'll tell my grandchildren:

"You know, we called it cloud computing long before the cloud was actually above our heads."

And they'll probably think I'm making it up.

No Photoshop. No Aseprite. No pre-made image assets.

Just Claude Code, JavaScript, and a surprisingly effective creative workflow.

Meet PixelFX, an open-source collection of 244 code-generated pixel art effects, complete with a Claude Code skill that helps you create your own.

And some of these animations look genuinely fantastic.

Here's what you'll find:

Fire and explosions: Flames, smoke, sparks, and magical fireballs

Magic and combat: Lightning, ice spells, energy beams, and sword attacks

Weather effects: Rain, snow, clouds, and atmospheric particles

Character animations: Movement, impacts, status effects, and attack sequences

UI animations: Achievements, notifications, transitions, and collectibles

Sci-fi effects: Force fields, holograms, energy cores, and glitches

And here's the interesting part.

Every animation is generated programmatically.

Instead of using existing sprites, the code calculates how pixels should appear and move over time.

That means you can change colors, adjust timing, modify particle behavior, and generate entirely new variations.

You can use the effects directly in JavaScript games or export them as sprite sheets for engines like Godot, Unity, and GameMaker.

But the real secret isn't the code. It's the process.

The project builds on a creative methodology shared by Hugo Duprez, the developer behind Sprite Fusion.

And his advice is surprisingly practical.

1. Treat code like clay.

Don't expect a perfect result from one prompt. Ask Claude to generate 5–10 variations, render them, and choose the most promising direction.

2. Trust your eyes.

AI can write the animation code, but you're still responsible for the creative direction. Refine the timing, movement, colors, and tiny details until the result actually feels right.

3. Feed your creativity.

Study great pixel art, games, films, and visual effects. Better references lead to better creative decisions.

PixelFX packages this approach into a reusable Claude Code skill.

Install it in Claude Code:

/plugin marketplace add patch-gg/pixelfx
/plugin install pixelfx@pixelfx

Then ask Claude to create something like:

"Create five variations of a magical ice explosion, render previews, and help me choose the best one for my pixel art game."

The skill can generate the effects, render previews, and help you refine them through multiple iterations.

And the whole project is free and open source under the MIT license.

What I particularly like about this approach is that AI isn't simply generating finished images.

It's generating the underlying systems that create the visuals.

And those systems can be edited, reused, and improved.

That's a much more interesting direction for AI-assisted game development.

Not by donating money. Not by watching an advertisement.

Meet FireCatchers, one of the smartest examples of creative marketing I've seen recently.

Developed by Havas Play and Sapeurs-Pompiers de France, the campaign transforms Twitch's ordinary "Starting Soon" screens into a real-time wildfire detection network.

And the idea is brilliantly simple.

Here's how it works:

Live forest cameras: Instead of a boring waiting screen, viewers see live footage from wildfire-prone areas in France.

Community-powered detection: Gamers watch for suspicious smoke while waiting for their stream to begin.

Instant reporting: If someone spots something unusual, they report the camera number in Twitch chat.

Human verification: When multiple viewers flag the same camera, an alert goes to the local emergency operations center for verification.

Real-world impact: Viewers become part of an early-warning system that can help firefighters respond faster.

The campaign launched in July 2025 with four French Twitch creators.

And according to the campaign's published results, it achieved:

600,000 followers reached through participating creators

786 additional streamers joining voluntarily

2,190 hours of additional live surveillance

5 fires detected

But here's why I find this particularly interesting from a marketing perspective.

This isn't advertising disguised as entertainment. It's entertainment infrastructure repurposed for something genuinely useful.

Havas Play didn't interrupt the audience with another banner.

They found a moment when people were already paying attention and gave that attention a purpose.

They didn't ask gamers to become passive supporters of a campaign.

They gave them an actual role.

And suddenly, an ordinary Twitch waiting screen became a community-powered public safety tool.

That's a pretty powerful lesson for brands, marketers, and anyone working on partnerships.

The best brand collaborations don't just ask for attention. They give people something meaningful to do with it.

Sometimes the most creative media placement isn't about finding a new place to advertise.

items.videoDescription:
What if you could make Claude Code more efficient by giving each AI model a different job?
Instead of using the most expensive model for everything, try a smarter multi-model setup:
Sonnet does the coding. Opus provides expert advice. Haiku explores the codebase.
Three models. Three roles. One coordinated workflow.

Here's how it works:
- Claude Sonnet: Your main coding agent. Handles implementation, edits, testing, and everyday development.
- Claude Opus: Your senior advisor. Reviews complex decisions, helps solve difficult problems, and provides guidance when Sonnet gets stuck.
- Claude Haiku: Your research assistant. Explores repositories, reads files, searches for dependencies, and reports findings.

The goal? Better resource allocation, potentially lower costs, and less unnecessary work for your most powerful models.

Step 1: Install the multi-model configuration
npx claude-code-templates@latest --setting model/sonnet-opus-advisor-haiku-subagents

During installation, choose where the settings should apply: User, Project, or Local.

Step 2: Make your Haiku subagents read-only
Here's an additional improvement I recommend.
When Haiku subagents investigate your codebase, they don't necessarily need permission to modify anything.
Let them research. Let Sonnet make the changes.

You can enforce this behavior using two Claude Code hooks:
Subagents Explore Only: Uses SubagentStart to instruct subagents to investigate and report findings without modifying files.
Subagent Read Only Guard: Uses PreToolUse to block common file-writing tools and state-changing commands when invoked by subagents.

Install both:
npx claude-code-templates@latest --setting hooks/subagents-explore-only --hook security/subagent-read-only-guard

Your main agent keeps its normal permissions, while research subagents work under additional restrictions. Note that the guard does not cover every possible write mechanism, including write-capable MCP tools.

 DEV Community
Why does this matter?
Because more powerful AI models aren't always the answer.
Sometimes the biggest improvement comes from giving the right task to the right model.
Let Haiku do the research.
Let Sonnet do the work.
Let Opus handle the hard questions.
Save this configuration and try it in your next Claude Code session.

items.excerpt: What if AI could do more than generate a 3D model? What if it could actually figure out how to build one? Meet SKY-001 by Skyfall AI, a new engineering world model designed to turn text prompts and reference images into
items.videoDescription:
What if AI could do more than generate a 3D model?
What if it could actually figure out how to build one?
Meet SKY-001 by Skyfall AI, a new engineering world model designed to turn text prompts and reference images into detailed mechanical assemblies.
And the team behind it has a fascinating history.
Back in 2017, Microsoft acquired Maluuba, an AI startup founded by Sam Pasupalak and Kaheer Suleman.

That was a year before OpenAI released GPT-1.
Now the founders are back with Skyfall AI. And instead of building another large language model, they've created something very different.
An AI model that reasons about how physical objects are constructed.

Here's how SKY-001 works:
- Starts with a text description or reference image
- Generates an initial 3D design
- Breaks complex objects into individual components
- Decomposes assemblies down to tiny screws and fasteners
- Creates 2D engineering sketches and 3D construction sequences
- Assembles the components into a complete mechanical structure
- Supports CAD-oriented workflows, including demonstrations involving Autodesk Fusion
And the results are pretty wild.
According to Skyfall AI's own benchmarks:
- 51× faster than GPT-6 Astra on CAD construction tasks
- 150× cheaper per CAD construction case
- Comparable geometric accuracy: 79.7% versus Astra's 79.1%
- Even larger speed improvements on certain BIM tasks

These are company-reported results, not yet independently verified. SKY-001 is currently a research preview with waitlist access.
But here's the part that really caught my attention.
Watch the moment when individual components start coming together, piece by piece, until they form a complete machine.
This isn't just AI producing a pretty 3D mesh.
It's attempting to understand the structure of an engineered object and generate the steps needed to construct it.
And that's a fundamentally different direction for generative AI.

We've seen models that write code, generate images, create videos, and simulate virtual worlds.
Now we're starting to see models designed to engineer objects in the physical world.
From generating pixels to designing machines.
That's a pretty significant leap.

https://skyfall.ai/sky-001

https://skyfall.ai/blog/introducing-sky-001

items.videoDescription:
What if AI could generate an entire world while you're exploring it?
Not a video. Not a traditional game. An interactive environment that responds to your actions in real time.
Meet Odyssey-3, a new AI world model that generates environments from text prompts or images and lets you explore them as they evolve.
And yes, you can apparently become a seal, a cat, or someone kayaking through an AI-generated world. Walking like a normal human is also an option, although considerably less interesting.

What Odyssey-3 can do:
- Generate interactive 3D-like environments from text prompts
- Use images as starting points for new worlds
- Let you explore in first-person or third-person view
- Move the camera independently
- Introduce new events while the world is being generated
- Predict how objects move and interact using learned physics
But here's where things get interesting.

Odyssey-3 Pro scored 66.1 on Physics-IQ Verified, achieving the highest reported video-to-video benchmark result using best-of-8 sampling.
The benchmark tests how accurately AI models predict the continuation of real physical experiments, covering everything from fluid dynamics to optics and mechanics.
And Odyssey isn't building this technology just for entertainment.

The company is exploring applications in robotics, autonomous vehicles, and AI agents that need to understand and interact with physical environments.
I tried Odyssey-3 Flash in the browser.
The waiting time was around five minutes. Then I got roughly five minutes to explore before being sent back to the queue.
Five minutes to play God. Five minutes to wait. Apparently, even AI-generated universes have capacity limits.
Still, this is a fascinating glimpse of a future where worlds aren't designed in advance. They're generated as you experience them.

And what if that made them dramatically faster and cheaper?

Meet Pomerado, a new Y Combinator startup that's taking a completely different approach to browser automation.

And the results are pretty ridiculous.

Here's the problem.

Most AI agents use websites the same way humans do.

They open a browser, find buttons, click around, read the screen, and repeat.

It works. But it's slow, expensive, and surprisingly fragile.

Pomerado does something smarter.

Instead of forcing your AI agent to navigate the same interface every time, it explores the website once and builds a reusable API or MCP integration.

Then your agent can call that integration directly.

No endless screenshots. No repeated visual navigation. No unnecessary reasoning about where to click next.

And when the website changes?

Pomerado's managed platform can detect broken integrations and automatically repair them.

Now for the really interesting part.

In a demonstration involving onboarding two employees across several business systems:

Codex Computer Use: 21 minutes 22 seconds, $41.01

Pomerado: 8 minutes 16 seconds, $0.03

That's approximately 2.6× faster and 1,367× cheaper in this particular test.

Yes. Three cents instead of forty-one dollars.

These are company-reported results, not independent benchmarks, but they're certainly worth investigating.

What else can Pomerado do?

Turn websites without public APIs into reusable tools

Connect to Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, and other MCP-compatible agents

Work with legacy CRMs, ERPs, internal dashboards, and business portals

Handle authenticated workflows, including two-factor authentication

Generate integrations from natural-language instructions

Automatically repair broken integrations through its managed cloud service

And here's the best part.

The core technology is open source under the MIT license.

You can build and run integrations locally, although creating them requires an OpenAI API key. The hosted service adds authentication management, hosting, and automatic maintenance.

This could be a significant development for agentic automation.

Because the future of AI agents might not involve making them better at clicking buttons.

DeepSeek took a completely different approach.

Its environment was absolutely stunning, with beautiful scenery and atmosphere. But there was one small problem.

The koi fish.

Let's just say the fish weren't quite as convincing as the rest of the scene.

Astra delivered speed, precision, and originality at a premium price.

DeepSeek delivered remarkable environmental design at a fraction of the cost, but needed significantly more time and struggled with some details.

Of course, this is a single creative experiment, not a comprehensive benchmark.

But it illustrates something important about AI-assisted creative work.

The most expensive model doesn't necessarily produce the most interesting result. And the cheapest model isn't necessarily the best value if time matters.

Sometimes the real question isn't which AI model is smarter.

It's which one you actually prefer looking at.

items.videoDescription:
How many follow-ups would you send before giving up on your dream customer?

Three? Five? Maybe ten?

Well, Harry Stebbings sent 53 emails to Marc Benioff, the CEO of Salesforce.

And for 52 weeks, he got absolutely nothing.

Not a single reply.

If you don't know Harry, he's the founder of 20VC, one of the most influential venture capital podcasts, and the man behind a VC firm that raised a $400 million fund.

He started his podcast at just 18.

I've known of Harry since my student days in London, back when I was struggling to sell the first subscriptions to my startup, Jammy, while he was already making waves in the startup ecosystem.

And his approach to cold outreach is a masterclass in persistence.

Here's what he did:

Every Sunday evening, at the same time, Harry emailed Marc Benioff asking him to appear on his podcast.

But he didn't just send the same boring "Just following up" message 53 times.

He did his homework.

Every email included a different, highly personalized P.S.

Benioff's favorite whiskey

His favorite vacation destinations

His food preferences

Salesforce's latest quarterly results

Personal details that demonstrated genuine research

He even A/B tested different approaches.

The result after 52 weeks? Absolutely nothing.

Until one particular email mentioned Benioff's favorite Macallan whiskey.

And suddenly, Marc replied.

He agreed to appear on the show.

Benioff later acknowledged that Harry had emailed and texted him nearly 100 times before getting a yes.

His conclusion?

"Persistence pays."

And that's the lesson for startup founders.

Especially if you're selling to mid-market or enterprise customers with a relatively small target account list.

You can't afford to give up after a couple of unanswered emails.

But here's the important distinction.

Persistence isn't sending the same message over and over. It's finding a new reason to be relevant every time.

My favorite GTM formula for 2026:

Founder-Led + Signal-Based + Multichannel + Creative Storytelling + AI

Research your accounts. Understand their priorities. Find meaningful signals. Make every interaction count.

And respect clear boundaries. Persistence should never become harassment.

Now open your CRM and look at your biggest opportunity.

How many attempts did you make before giving up?

Because Harry was apparently just getting warmed up.

Claude can already generate animations and videos. But there's always been one annoying problem.
What happens when you want to actually edit the result?
An AI-generated MP4 isn't an editable Premiere Pro timeline. You can't just open it in After Effects and start adjusting individual layers, animations, or keyframes.
Well, that gap is finally starting to close.
Meet Tesseract by Mirage, a creative toolkit that lets AI agents create, edit, and export projects compatible with Adobe Premiere Pro and After Effects.
And the interesting part? Your AI agent can work directly with editable project files without controlling a graphical interface.

Here's what Tesseract can do:
- Create videos and motion graphics through AI agents
- Export editable Premiere Pro projects (.prproj)
- Export After Effects compositions (.aep)
- Import existing Adobe projects for AI-assisted editing
- Modify supported timelines, layers, and animations
- Render finished videos without an Adobe subscription
- Work through code and structured project files instead of mouse clicks and screenshots

The project converters are also open source under the MIT license.
There are some limitations: format support is still partial, and After Effects export is experimental. Complex effects, fonts, and animations may not transfer perfectly. Mirage
But the bigger picture is fascinating.
Until recently, AI-generated creative work often ended with a finished file you couldn't meaningfully modify.
Now we're moving toward AI agents producing real, editable creative projects that humans can continue working on.

Imagine asking Claude to create a motion graphics sequence, opening the result in After Effects, adjusting a few keyframes, and finishing it yourself.
Or doing the reverse: giving an existing Premiere Pro project to an AI agent and asking it to make changes.
AI handles the production. You keep creative control.
That's a much more interesting future for AI-assisted video production than simply generating another MP4.

items.videoDescription:
What if you could run a powerful AI video generation model on your own computer, without renting expensive cloud GPUs?

And what if you only needed 8 GB of VRAM?

Meet FreeVideo, an open-source project designed to bring MiniMax H3 video generation to consumer hardware.

Yes, the same family of AI video models usually associated with powerful GPU servers.

Except this time, you can run it locally.

Here's what FreeVideo offers:

8 GB VRAM + 16 GB RAM: The developers' claimed minimum hardware requirements.

MiniMax H3: AI video generation powered by the 8-step VDN-H3 model.

ComfyUI integration: Generate and customize videos through familiar workflows.

LoRA support: Customize generation with community LoRAs.

First and last frame control: Guide how your videos begin and end.

Multimodal references: Use images, videos, and audio as references.

Windows installer: Automatically installs the environment and downloads the necessary models.

Local processing: Generate videos on your own hardware.

But how fast is it really?

The developers published some interesting benchmarks.

For a 10-second video at 1344×768 resolution on Windows:

RTX 5090 (32 GB VRAM): 122 seconds

RTX 5060 Ti (16 GB VRAM): 486 seconds

RTX 4060 Ti (16 GB VRAM): 558 seconds

So yes, we're talking about roughly eight minutes to generate ten seconds of video on an RTX 5060 Ti.

Not exactly real-time generation.

But here's an important detail.

The developers also report 13.8 seconds per sampling step for an 8 GB VRAM and 16 GB RAM configuration.

There's a catch: That measurement was performed on an NVIDIA H200 with artificially restricted memory, not an actual consumer 8 GB graphics card.

A complete end-to-end benchmark for the minimum 8 GB VRAM + 16 GB RAM configuration hasn't been published in the official documentation.

So treat the minimum requirements as a promising technical claim, not a guarantee of practical performance on every home PC.

How does FreeVideo make this possible?

Under the hood, it uses Video DeltaNet's hybrid attention architecture and an adaptive execution engine.

Instead of trying to squeeze the entire model into GPU memory, FreeVideo distributes model weights across VRAM, system RAM, and disk, loading what it needs during generation.

And that's what makes this project interesting.

AI video generation is gradually moving from expensive cloud infrastructure to hardware people already own.

It might take several minutes to generate a short clip today.

items.excerpt: What if your AI agents could use your entire computer without constantly taking screenshots, analyzing pixels, and moving your mouse around? And what if multiple agents could work while you continued using your computer?
items.videoDescription:
What if your AI agents could use your entire computer without constantly taking screenshots, analyzing pixels, and moving your mouse around?

And what if multiple agents could work while you continued using your computer?

Meet agent-desktop, a new open-source project from Vercel Labs that brings the efficient approach of agent-browser to desktop automation.

And this could be a significant improvement for AI computer use.

Here's the problem.

Traditional computer-use agents often behave like humans.

They take a screenshot, analyze the image, figure out where to click, move the mouse, and repeat.

It works, but the process can be slow, expensive, and surprisingly fragile.

Agent Desktop takes a different approach.

Instead of relying on screenshots, it reads the operating system's native accessibility tree.

That gives AI agents structured information about what's actually on your screen:

Buttons and menus: Identify interactive elements directly.

Text fields: Read and modify supported interface elements.

Windows and applications: Navigate between desktop apps.

Stable element references: Interact with specific controls instead of guessing pixel coordinates.

Structured JSON: Give AI agents compact, machine-readable interface information.

And here's where things get really interesting.

Agent Desktop supports headless interactions.

That means supported actions can run through accessibility APIs without moving your physical mouse pointer or stealing focus.

Your AI agent can work in the background while you keep using your computer.

And there's more.

Multiple agents can share the same desktop environment.

Each agent can have its own visual cursor overlay, making it possible to see where different agents are working.

These are virtual cursor indicators, not independent physical mouse pointers. Operations requiring real mouse input are coordinated to avoid conflicts.

But the possibilities are fascinating.

Imagine one agent inspecting a spreadsheet while another works with your development tools, and a third handles a desktop application.

All coordinated through structured interfaces rather than endless screenshots.

Why does this matter?

Because computer use has been one of the most expensive and unreliable parts of AI automation.

Reading structured interface data instead of repeatedly processing screenshots could significantly reduce the amount of information an agent needs to handle.

And make desktop automation more predictable.

What else is included?

Native Rust implementation

Support for macOS, Windows, and Linux

CLI and C library interfaces

Integration with AI coding agents such as Claude Code and Codex

Session management, traces, and verification tools

Optional screenshots for visual workflows

Open-source Apache 2.0 license

Install Agent Desktop:

npm install -g agent-desktop

Check the installation:

agent-desktop version

On macOS, enable the required Accessibility permissions:

agent-desktop permissions --guide

You can also install the agent skill:

npx skills add https://github.com/vercel-labs/agent-desktop --skill agent-desktop

Of course, accessibility-based automation has limitations. Some applications don't expose every interface element, and certain actions may still require traditional mouse input or screenshots.

And desktop automation still requires carefully managed permissions, especially when agents can access sensitive applications.

But the direction is extremely interesting.

We're moving from AI agents that watch your computer to AI agents that understand its interface.

And maybe the future of computer use isn't teaching AI to click faster.

It's teaching AI that clicking like a human was never the best approach in the first place.

Editing existing images without ruining everything else.

Although there's a catch.

Its image editing capabilities look considerably more convincing than some of its text-to-image results, where artifacts can still be noticeable.

And despite the speed improvements, we're not quite at real-time editing yet.

So which one is more interesting?

FLUX 3 Image Klein is compelling if you want local generation, model customization, low API costs, and more control over image composition.

Krea 3 looks especially useful if you're editing existing visuals and need fast, consistent results.

But here's the bigger picture.

AI image generation is getting cheaper. AI image editing is getting faster. And the difference between generating an image and actually working with it is finally starting to disappear.

At this rate, spending several minutes waiting for a single AI image edit will soon feel positively prehistoric.

The task? Working with 60 videos simultaneously.
Claude decided that the most efficient way for me to review the results was to put all 60 videos on a single screen.

At once.
With everyone talking.

Welcome to the future of human-AI collaboration.

items.excerpt: Your AI coding agent just modified 15 files, added 800 lines of code, and proudly announced: "All done. Everything works." Great. But do you actually understand what it changed? Meet diff-tour, a free, open-source tool t
items.videoDescription:
Your AI coding agent just modified 15 files, added 800 lines of code, and proudly announced:

"All done. Everything works."

Great.

But do you actually understand what it changed?

Meet diff-tour, a free, open-source tool that walks you through code changes the way an experienced software engineer would review them.

It works with Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, and other AI coding assistants.

And instead of dumping a giant Git diff in front of you, it creates an interactive, step-by-step explanation.

Here's what diff-tour does:

Explains the big picture: Why the changes were made and how they fit into your existing codebase.

Shows what matters: Highlights the files you should examine, including related files that weren't modified.

Asks the right questions: What happens if something fails? Can this safely run twice? Will existing functionality still work?

Identifies real problems: Separates must-fix issues from optional improvements and explains why suspicious-looking code might actually be safe.

Teaches you to think like a senior engineer: Sometimes it asks you to predict what could go wrong before revealing the explanation.

Uses actual Git data: Every displayed line of repository code comes directly from Git, not from something the AI invented.

And here's the interesting part.

The entire review runs in read-only mode.

Your AI agent can inspect and explain the code, but it cannot modify your repository during the tour.

The tool uses your existing Claude Code or Codex account, and generating a review typically takes around 2–5 minutes, according to the developers.

How to install diff-tour on macOS or Linux:

curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/init-co-jp/diff-tour/main/install.sh | sh

Then navigate to your Git project and run:

tour

Choose the changes you want to review and let the walkthrough begin.

You can navigate between explanations, explore code, answer questions, and investigate potential problems before merging anything.

My suggestion: add this to your AI coding workflow.

Let Claude Code or Codex implement a feature.

Run tour to understand the changes.

Identify the issues that actually need fixing.

Give those findings to Claude Opus 5.5.

Ask it to explain its proposed fixes before touching any code.

Approve the changes, run the tests, and review the final diff.

Here's a prompt you can use with Opus 5.5 after the review:

"diff-tour reviewed my latest code changes and identified these must-fix issues:

[PASTE FINDINGS HERE]

For each issue, explain how you plan to fix it and which files you'll modify. Wait for my approval before making any changes.

Once approved, implement the fixes, run the relevant tests, and report which issues are resolved and which remain."

Of course, an AI-generated review doesn't replace proper testing or human judgment.

But it gives you something increasingly valuable in the age of agentic coding.

Understanding.

Because generating code is getting ridiculously easy.

Understanding, maintaining, and safely shipping that code is still your responsibility.

And frankly, having a patient senior-engineer-style walkthrough every time your AI agent finishes a task sounds pretty useful.

Free, open source, MIT licensed.

items.videoDescription:
This wasn't drawn by a human.
And it wasn't generated by a traditional AI video model either.
Claude Opus 5.5 wrote code that generated every single frame of this 32-second animation.
No hand-drawn frames. No manual keyframe animation. Just AI-written code turning mathematics, physics, and creative ideas into moving images.
And the result is quite a journey.

In just 32 seconds, you'll see:
- A playful little animated cube
- Planets moving through cosmic orbits
- White light splitting into colors through a prism
- A swirling vortex of particles
- A black hole bending space and light
- A breathtaking view of Earth from the Moon
Every scene was generated programmatically.

That's what makes this experiment interesting.
We're used to AI generating videos by predicting pixels. But AI coding models can take a completely different approach: write the algorithms that create the visuals themselves.

Procedural animation. Mathematics. Particle systems. Simulated physics. All orchestrated through code.
And unlike a conventional AI-generated video, code-based animation can potentially be modified, extended, and reproduced by changing the underlying instructions.
32 seconds. Six visual worlds. Every frame created by AI-written code.
The future of motion design might involve a lot more programming than drawing.

items.videoDescription:
Apparently, Unitree decided that the best way to introduce its new humanoid robot was to make an action movie.

And honestly, I'm not complaining.

Meet Unitree H2-X Kung Fu Legend Guardian, a humanoid robot that looks like it walked straight out of a sci-fi blockbuster.

In the official demonstration, it:

Punches and kicks car doors, leaving visible damage

Performs backflips and martial arts moves

Jumps from a 4-meter-high platform

Confronts an armed attacker in a staged security scenario

Pushes a mannequin away from an approaching car

Lifts the front of a vehicle in a simulated rescue operation

Yes, apparently, robot bodyguards now come with their own stunt choreography.

And Unitree claims up to 8 hours of endurance.

There's a catch, though.

That figure refers to standing endurance, not eight hours of continuous kung fu.

The company also hasn't explained whether these impressive moves were performed autonomously, remotely controlled, or through preprogrammed sequences.

So while the hardware looks extraordinary, we're not quite at the point where you can hire a robot to independently handle your personal security.

And I have to admit, the rescue scene raised a few questions.

I'm not entirely sure the mannequin survived the robot's rescue attempt any better than the approaching car.

But my favorite part?

After showing us a humanoid machine smashing cars, jumping four meters, and fighting attackers, Unitree ends with a friendly reminder:

Please use the robot safely and in a friendly manner.

Of course. What could possibly go wrong?
